KEY MESSAGE 1...Lingering showers this morning towards the southern 
coast, Cape Cod, and the Islands. Otherwise, drier and colder today.

Showers over much of SE MA and RI continue this morning with the 
cold front associated with a low pressure system now over New 
Brunswick, Canada draped over the southern portion of the south 
shore down into coastal RI. This front will continue eastward early 
this morning, and we will find ourselves in a much colder and drier 
airmass with high pressure starting to build in from the west. These 
showers should remain generally over SE MA, Cape Cod, the Islands, 
and parts of RI this morning, then drop off more towards the 
afternoon as the drier air behind this front really sets in. Skies 
will clear more towards the evening, especially with high pressure 
taking more of a hold overhead by then. Gusty NW winds today as 
strong cold air advection develops and the gradient between the 
exiting low pressure to our northeast and the high pressure to our 
west tightens, which may reach up to 35 mph in some areas this 
afternoon. 925 mb temperatures fall below 0C by this evening, and 
prior to that mark, they look to hover just above it. Highs today 
will likely struggle to reach the low 50s across the interior and 
lows Saturday night will likely dip below freezing across the 
region, with the exceptions being areas closest to the coasts and 
urban areas. Once the gusty NW winds diminish later this evening, we 
could see some radiational cooling develop as high pressure builds 
in post-FROPA, enhancing an already relatively cold night for some 
locations. Areas of frost/freezing conditions are anticipated, 
though because our program came to an end on October 11, there will 
be no Frost/Freeze headlines issued.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Dry with a modest warmup through mid next week, but 
monitoring stormy conditions near or south of the mid-Atlantic 
waters which could bring periods of light rain, enhanced northeast 
winds, and building waves/possible erosion to southeast New England.

High pressure continues to build in Sunday and the colder airmass 
shifts out of the region. The tighter gradient between the strong 
exiting low and approaching high pressure slackens, which will allow 
winds to continue diminishing as well. As high pressure settles in 
overhead, temperatures will moderate back to more typical levels for 
this time of year as 850 mb temperatures improve from -5C today to 
around +5C by Sunday evening. 925 mb temperatures steadily increase 
as well, reaching around +10C towards the Monday/Tuesday 
timeframe. Highs return to the 50s and 60s into early next week. 

One thing we will be keeping an eye on, though, is the development 
of low pressure towards the mid-Atlantic/Carolina coastal waters 
Sunday into Monday. This feature appears to have detached from the 
broader upper level trough that was associated with the strong low 
pressure that brought yesterday's precipitation. Guidance is 
indicating that a weaker spot in the surface ridge over southern New 
England may allow for some showers to sneak in sometime 
Monday/Tuesday over southeastern New England. Given the dry 
conditions preceding these possible showers, QPF looks quite 
limited, with ensemble probabilities for any measurable rainfall 
mostly between 10-50%, with the GEFS and Canadian ENS skewing 
slightly higher over the Cape and Islands at 50-60%. The ECMWF 
ensemble is the lowest of the three, with the highest probabilities 
over land being 10-30%. However, marine impacts with this 
disturbance are looking a bit more impactful as it stays relatively 
stationary and churns over the same waters for an extended period of 
time, which will help build seas up to 15 ft offshore of Nantucket.
 
The gradient between this area of low pressure and the preexisting 
high pressure over southern New England will tighten greatly, 
increasing ENE winds over the waters and towards the Cape and 
Islands, RI, and the coastal plain in SE MA. Ensembles have 
continued to indicate decent probabilities of sustained winds 
reaching gale-force over the southern waters, with the GEFS and 
Canadian ensemble up to 30-40% (and even up to 60% in the Canadian 
guidance) just south of the Islands. In terms of gale-force gusts, 
probabilities have increased further from the last update, reaching 
the high (80-100%) range in the ECMWF ensemble and up to 80% in the 
GEFS. Persistent easterly fetch associated with these winds, along 
with building rough seas, will need to be monitored as well, as 
beach erosion for east- and northeast-facing beaches may become an 
issue.
